name: June Harrow
equipment: Concealable Aramid vest (department issue) under a tan uniform shirt
Remington 700 .308 bolt-action rifle with a 3-9x scope (5-round magazine)
Missouri Department of Conservation badge and ID
Topographic map of Haskett County, annotated in pencil
features: Human Versatility (Human: +1 to all ability scores)
Overwatch (reaction: when an enemy you can see moves within your weapon's normal range, make one ranged attack against it; once per short rest)
Trailwise (advantage on Survival checks to track and navigate; the party cannot be surprised while she is on watch and conscious)
Proficiencies (Melee, Sidearms, Longarms; Light and Medium armor)

Badge and Authority (Police Officer feature: as a state conservation agent she has legal authority anywhere in the county; people who still respect the law will answer her questions and let her through)

personality.traits: I say very little and notice everything. I can sit still in a tree stand for six hours and I can tell you what walked past it. I write things down.
personality.ideals: The law is just people agreeing to be decent to each other when they don't have to be. Somebody has to keep agreeing.
personality.bonds: I know every back road, creek crossing and deer trail in this county. It is mine to look after, and right now it needs looking after more than it ever has.
personality.flaws: I am stubborn past the point of sense. Once I decide someone is lying to me I will not let it go, and I am not always right.

appearance: Forty, tall and rangy, with weathered skin, crow's feet and a grey-streaked brown braid. Wears a tan Conservation Department uniform shirt and green trousers, a ballcap, and a rifle sling worn shiny. Has a slow, deliberate way of turning her head, as if listening to something far away.
backstory: June Harrow has been the Missouri Department of Conservation agent for Haskett County for eleven years: poachers, boating accidents, a meth lab in a deer camp, a lot of lost hunters and one drowned child she still thinks about. She knows every landowner, every gravel road and every ford on the Tamarack. She was off duty at Ferry Days with her rifle locked in her state truck, buying sweet corn, and she was the first person on Front Street to understand that the woman in the volunteer T-shirt walking toward the crowd was not a woman any more — because she had seen the way a deer with chronic wasting disease walks, and this was the same.
